AE Grading Report

gsm.kri Example

September 01, 2026 14:35:36 UTC

Set Up

This page provides a sample AE Grading Report generated using the gsm.kri package. Expand the “Setup” section below to see the code used to generate the report. Or scroll down for the standard report output.

The report is a companion to the two site-level grading metrics, kri0016 (High-Grade AE Proportion) and kri0017 (Low-Grade AE Proportion). Those metrics flag sites whose overall severity mix differs from the study; this report adds the term-level detail they cannot show.

Note on the example data. The gsm.core example data carries only two placeholder preferred terms (term1, term2) and no site-level grading behaviour, so it cannot demonstrate the term-level analysis. This page therefore simulates the AE severity grades and preferred terms with Sim_AEGrading(), keeping the real subject/site structure and per-site AE burden. A handful of sites are given deliberate grading patterns so the report has something to find. Every number below is illustrative; the mechanics are real.

Setup 
# Load libraries
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(tibble)
library(gsm.core)
library(gsm.kri)
library(gsm.mapping)

source("util/Sim_AEGrading.R")

# Map the example source data
mappings_wf <- workr::MakeWorkflowList(
  strNames = c("AE", "SUBJ", "SITE", "STUDY", "ENROLL", "COUNTRY", "DATAENT"),
  strPath = "workflow/1_mappings",
  strPackage = "gsm.mapping"
)

mappings_spec <- gsm.mapping::CombineSpecs(mappings_wf)
lRaw <- gsm.mapping::Ingest(gsm.core::lSource, mappings_spec)

# Simulate a realistic grading scenario over the real site structure
sim <- Sim_AEGrading(mapped$Mapped_AE, mapped$Mapped_SUBJ)
mapped$Mapped_AE <- sim$AE

# Run the High-Grade AE Proportion metric so the report can mark flagged sites
kri0016 <- workr::RunWorkflow(
  workr::MakeWorkflowList("kri0016", strPath = "workflow/2_metrics", strPackage = "gsm.kri")[[1]],
  mapped
)

AE Grading Overview

Study: AA-AA-000-0000 Report generated: 01 September 2026

This report examines how consistently investigator sites apply CTCAE severity grading to adverse events. It is a companion to the two site-level grading KRIs (kri0016 High-Grade AE Proportion and kri0017 Low-Grade AE Proportion) and adds the term-level detail those aggregate metrics cannot show.

It looks at grading from two angles:

  1. Overall severity mix — does a site’s distribution of Grade 1–5 events look like the rest of the study? This catches sites that grade nearly everything as Grade 1, or nearly everything as Grade 3/4.
  2. Term-level consistency — for the most commonly reported preferred terms, does the site grade the same event the way the rest of the study does? This catches sites whose overall mix looks unremarkable but who apply the criteria inconsistently from one term to the next.

6573 graded adverse events across 97 sites met the minimum volume threshold of 20 graded AEs per site. Study-wide, 22.5% of adverse events are Grade 3 or higher.

Term-level grading consistency

The overall severity mix is a blunt instrument: a site can report a perfectly average proportion of severe events while still grading individual event types inconsistently. This section compares each site against the study for the 10 most frequently reported preferred terms, so a site’s case mix cannot be mistaken for a grading difference.

Evaluation rules

  • A preferred term is evaluated if it has at least 50 events study-wide.
  • A site is evaluated on that term if it reported at least 10 events of it.
  • A site/term pair is flagged when its Grade 3+ proportion differs from the study-wide proportion for that term by at least 20% (in either direction).
  • A site is raised for investigation when it is flagged on two or more terms.

Method notes and limitations

  • Grades are treated as reported. No re-derivation from lab values or outcome data is attempted; the report measures internal consistency across sites, not clinical correctness.
  • The study is its own comparator. If grading drifts study-wide, this report will not detect it — every site is compared to the study average.
  • The absolute-difference rule is asymmetric in practice. Because the study-wide Grade 3+ proportion is only 22.5%, a site cannot fall 20% below the study average on a term whose study-wide Grade 3+ proportion is itself under 20%. Under-grading on low-severity terms is therefore structurally hard to flag with a fixed percentage-point rule. The z column applies a volume-scaled binomial z-score instead, which stays symmetric across both tails; it is reported alongside the absolute rule so the two can be compared before a production threshold is chosen.
  • Volume thresholds bind hard at small sites. Sites below 10 events for a term are not evaluated on it, so a small site with a genuine grading problem may show no flags at all.
  • Multiplicity is not controlled. With 10 terms and 97 sites, some flagged pairs are expected by chance alone. Requiring two or more flagged terms per site is a deliberately crude guard against this.
